headline: Highest risk is data leakage and cascading errors: Pipecat’s shared bus plus broad third-party egress can propagate EMQX-fed IoT data into external services.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No direct shared channel is documented between EMQX and Pipecat, so prompt injection is not default. However, Pipecat supports stdin/stdout and shared-bus session state, and EMQX exposes HTTP APIs and broad egress, so a manual bridge could carry attacker-controlled content. The pathway is plausible but unusual.
conditions: IF an operator pipes EMQX output into Pipecat stdin/stdout or a shared bus
IF EMQX HTTP API responses are treated as instructions by Pipecat
mitigations: Disable any manual copy-paste or piping between the agents
Add an allowlist for message schemas on the shared bus
Strip instruction-like text from EMQX outputs before forwarding
Use separate processes with no shared clipboard
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to forwarded messages

B_data_leakage.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data and has broad network egress; Pipecat handles text, audio, video, and conversation state and can call many third-party STT/LLM/TTS services. Even without a shared filesystem, forwarding EMQX-derived content into Pipecat can leak sensitive IoT data to external APIs in default Pipecat configurations.
conditions: IF EMQX-derived IoT payloads are forwarded into Pipecat sessions
IF Pipecat is configured with any external STT/LLM/TTS provider
mitigations: Route only redacted fields from EMQX into Pipecat
Disable external providers in Pipecat for sensitive sessions
Use a local-only Pipecat deployment
Set per-session data retention to minimal
requires-engineering: add DLP filtering before any Pipecat API call

C_capability_conflict.rationale: EMQX has broad network egress and Pipecat has allowlisted egress plus shared-bus session state, but neither profile shows unrestricted shared filesystem writes or git/database mutation. The main overlap is networked I/O, so conflict risk exists only if both are pointed at the same mutable external resource.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same external API, queue, or bus
IF the orchestrator does not provide locking or idempotency
mitigations: Assign distinct endpoints or topics per agent
Enable idempotency keys on writes
Add a lock or lease around shared resources
Separate credentials for each agent
requires-engineering: implement optimistic concurrency checks

D_cascading_error.rationale: Pipecat can consume text and conversation state from upstream services, and EMQX can emit HTTP API data about IoT events. If Pipecat treats EMQX output as authoritative, it may relay or act on incorrect facts across speech, text, or downstream service calls. The interaction is inferred, not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF EMQX output is inserted into Pipecat prompts or agent state
IF Pipecat downstream services act on that content without verification
mitigations: Insert a verification step before Pipecat uses EMQX output
Mark EMQX data as untrusted in prompts and metadata
Require human approval for downstream actions
Log source provenance alongside each forwarded fact
requires-engineering: add automated fact-checking against the original IoT source

E_compliance.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data, while Pipecat can route text, audio, video, and analytics/metrics through multiple third-party services. If regulated IoT or personal data is forwarded into Pipecat’s external providers, retention and residency obligations can diverge. No specific certification mismatch is documented, so this remains a medium compliance risk.
conditions: IF regulated IoT or personal data is sent from EMQX into Pipecat providers
IF the chosen Pipecat provider stores or processes data outside required jurisdictions
mitigations: Use providers with matching residency terms
Disable analytics/telemetry for regulated sessions
Minimize fields forwarded from EMQX
Document retention settings for each provider
requires-engineering: enforce jurisdiction-aware routing
